tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[BLOCKER] Half the natural-product SMILES strings are not valid SMILES and do not parse; the platform has no machine-readable chemistry — Four of the eight strings in the `smiles:` field of NATURAL_PRODUCTS_DATA are not chemical structures. RDKit 2026.3.5 `Chem.MolFromSmiles` returns None for all four, and returns None even with sanitize=False (i.e. these are tokenizer/graph-construction failures, not valence-sanitization failures).

(1) app.js:50 Curcumin — "COC1=C(C=CC(=C1)C=CC(=O)CC(=O)C=CC2=CC(=C(C=C2)O)OCH3)O". The substring "OCH3" at index 49 is chemical shorthand for a methoxy group, not SMILES. In SMILES a bare uppercase 'H' is not a legal atom token outside brackets, and the following '3' is parsed as ring-bond-closure label 3, which is never opened. The correct token for methoxy is "OC". Substituting s/OCH3/OC/ yields a molecule that parses to C21H20O6, InChIKey VFLDPWHFBUODDF-UHFFFAOYSA-N, whose skeleton block matches real curcumin (PubChem CID 969516, VFLDPWHFBUODDF-FCXRPNKRSA-N) — so this is a single-token typo that was never once run through a parser.

(2) app.js:10 Huperzine A — "CC1=CC2C(=C)C3C(=O)NC(=C2CC3(C)N)C". Ring-closure label 1 is opened at 'C1=' and never closed, leaving a dangling ring bond. Beyond the parse failure, the intended graph is not huperzine A: the real compound (PubChem CID 854026, C15H18N2O, MW 242.32) is a tricyclic 2-pyridone bearing an exocyclic (E)-ethylidene and a quaternary bridgehead amine — connectivity SMILES CC=C1C2CC3=C(C1(CC(=C2)C)N)C=CC(=O)N3. The app.js string encodes an exocyclic methylidene (C(=C)) rather than the ethylidene and has no pyridone ring fusion.

(3) app.js:60 Onjisaponin V — the `smiles:` field literally contains the text "C58H92O27 (Onjisaponin V Core Skeleton)".
(4) app.js:70 Salvianolic Acid B — the `smiles:` field literally contains "C36H30O16 (Caffeic Acid Tetramer)".

These last two are molecular formulas with a parenthetical English gloss placed in a structure field. A molecular formula specifies atom counts only; it carries zero connectivity and therefore cannot be converted to a molecular graph by any toolkit.

Grep over README.md, app.js, index.html and styles.css returns zero hits for rdkit, inchi, pubchem, chembl, openbabel, canonicalization, PAINS, logP, TPSA or Lipinski. The `smiles` field is read exactly once in the entire codebase, at app.js:477, where it is interpolated into innerHTML as a display string. Nothing ever parses it — which is precisely why four broken strings survived into a published repository. Consequence: The repository self-describes (README.md:22) as a 'state-of-the-art computational biology, structural pharmacology, and artificial intelligence-driven drug discovery platform', and index.html:118 advertises 'Detailed SMILES formulation'. A reader — a collaborator, a reviewer, or a funder — will reasonably infer that structures were validated and that descriptors, docking poses, or similarity searches were computed from them. None of that is possible: for four of eight compounds there is no molecule object to compute on, so no substructure search, no fingerprint, no descriptor, no docking, no PAINS filter, and no database cross-reference can ever have been run. Anyone who copies these strings into their own pipeline gets four hard failures and, worse, four silent misidentifications from the strings that do parse (see MEDCHEM-02, MEDCHEM-03).

text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-01: Replace all eight `smiles:` values with PubChem/ChEMBL isomeric SMILES and add a build-time gate that fails CI if any structure field does not round-trip: for each record, parse with RDKit, run the ChEMBL structure_pipeline Checker and Standardizer (Bento et al. 2020), compute the InChIKey, and assert it equals a stored expected InChIKey obtained from PubChem. Store the PubChem CID and ChEMBL ID alongside every compound as first-class fields. Never permit free text in a structure field — the schema should reject any `smiles` value for which MolFromSmiles returns None.

text:
[CRITICAL] The compound labelled 'Baicalein' is a different flavone — 6,7,8-trihydroxyflavone — and lacks the 5-OH/4-keto motif on which both stated mechanisms depend — The string at app.js:40, "C1=CC=C(C=C1)C2=CC(=O)C3=C(O2)C(=C(C(=C3)O)O)O", parses cleanly to C15H10O5 (MW 270.24) — the correct molecular formula for baicalein, which is presumably why the error went unnoticed. But it is the wrong constitutional isomer. I walked the fused benzo ring programmatically from the C4 carbonyl through C4a→C5→C6→C7→C8→C8a and found hydroxyls at C6, C7 and C8. Baicalein is 5,6,7-trihydroxyflavone; the app.js structure is 6,7,8-trihydroxyflavone.

InChIKeys confirm two distinct compounds: app.js string = SXZJEWVPXPKGJG-UHFFFAOYSA-N; real baicalein = FXNFHKRTJBSTCS-UHFFFAOYSA-N. An independent PubChem InChIKey lookup on SXZJEWVPXPKGJG-UHFFFAOYSA-N returns CID 14372623, IUPAC name '6,7,8-trihydroxy-2-phenylchromen-4-one' — a different registered substance from baicalein (CID 5281605, '5,6,7-trihydroxy-2-phenylchromen-4-one').

The specific hydroxyl that has been moved is the one that matters most. My substructure test confirms the app.js structure has no C5-OH, whereas real baicalein does. The C5-OH sits peri to the C4 ketone and forms the intramolecular hydrogen bond that defines the 5-hydroxy-4-keto chelation motif of flavones. Consequence: Both mechanisms the platform asserts for this compound run through the motif that has been deleted. app.js:42 claims '12/15-LOX catalytic Fe3+ chelation' — bidentate iron chelation by flavones is effected by the 5-OH/4-keto pair (and the catechol), and a 6,7,8-triol with a bare C5 cannot form that chelate. app.js:41-42 claims binding to the GSK-3beta ATP pocket at Val135/Asp133/Lys85, where the 5-OH/4-keto pair is the hinge-region donor-acceptor pair in flavone kinase inhibitors. An expert reading README.md:35 ('Lipophilic trihydroxyflavone. Targets GSK-3beta ATP pocket... and 12/15-LOX') would take the SMILES as the authoritative definition, feed SXZJEWVPXPKGJG into a docking run or a SAR series, and be optimizing the wrong chemotype. Because the molecular formula is right, this error survives every sanity check short of an actual InChIKey comparison — it is the most insidious class of structural error.

text:
[CRITICAL] Ginsenoside Rg1 and Ginkgolide B SMILES encode constitutionally wrong molecules whose formulas contradict the formulas asserted elsewhere in the same file — Both parseable saponin/terpenoid SMILES encode molecules with the wrong atom count and the wrong functional-group census, and in both cases the correct formula appears elsewhere in the same file — so the file is internally inconsistent with itself.

Ginsenoside Rg1 (app.js:20) parses to C38H64O14, MW 744.92, InChIKey skeleton DYTIXWQVBPQHKX. Real Rg1 is C42H72O14, MW 801.0, skeleton YURJSTAIMNSZAE (PubChem CID 441923) — a deficit of C4H8. app.js:142 itself states 'Ginsenoside Rg1 Dammarane-12,20-diol (C42H72O14)', the correct formula, contradicting the SMILES two hundred lines earlier. Two specific constitutional errors account for the discrepancy: (a) the C4 gem-dimethyl group that is diagnostic of the dammarane triterpene skeleton is absent — my SMARTS test for a ring quaternary carbon bearing two methyls returns False for the app.js string and True for real Rg1, and the methyl count is 5 versus 8; (b) the C20 sugar is attached through a carbon-carbon bond rather than a glycosidic oxygen. My anomeric-carbon analysis counts 1 O-glycosidic and 3 C-glycosidic anomeric carbons in the app.js string, versus 2 and 2 in real Rg1. An O-glycoside and a C-glycoside are different compound classes with different hydrolytic stability and completely different metabolic fate (C-glycosides resist glycosidase cleavage), so this is not a cosmetic difference.

Ginkgolide B (app.js:30) parses to C18H22O8, MW 366.37, skeleton KRGCYOMVCDUGIP, with 8 SSSR rings, 1 lactone and 1 ketone. Real ginkgolide B is C20H24O10, MW 424.4, skeleton SQOJOAFXDQDRGF (PubChem CID 11973122), hexacyclic with 3 lactones and 0 ketones. app.js:370 and README.md:34 both correctly describe it as a '6-ring tri-lactone cage' with formula C20H24O10 — the SMILES has 8 rings and one lactone. One of the three lactones has been replaced by a ketone and a ring has been mis-fused. The tert-butyl group is present in both, which is the only part of the described pharmacophore ('rigid 6-ring cage structure with a tert-butyl moiety', app.js:35) the SMILES actually delivers.

Two further asserted formulas are wrong: app.js:266 gives Ginsenoside Rg3 as 'C36H62O8' where PubChem gives C42H72O13 (MW 785.0); app.js:182 and app.js:328 give the presenegenin aglycone as 'C30H46O6' where PubChem CID 21594224 gives C30H46O7 (MW 518.7). Consequence: Rg1 and Ginkgolide B are the declared warheads for four of the twenty-five candidates (HippoTrk-Saponin-X1 at app.js:141-148, AstroZo1-Protect-A3 at app.js:369-376, and via Rg3 BasalNgf-TrkA-B3 at app.js:265-272 and BasalSuper-AChE-TrkA-B5 at app.js:285-292). Any property computed from these SMILES — mass, formula, logP, docking pose — describes a molecule that does not exist in Panax ginseng or Ginkgo biloba. The internal contradiction is itself diagnostic: the correct formulas were typed into the prose fields by hand while the SMILES were generated separately and never reconciled, which means no single automated pass ever validated formula against structure. A collaborator who trusts the prose and a collaborator who trusts the SMILES will build on two different molecules.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[BLOCKER] Every structure in the platform is stereochemically flat, so each saponin/terpenoid record denotes millions of distinct molecules rather than one — Not one of the eight structure fields carries a single stereodescriptor. There are no '@'/'@@' tetrahedral tags and no '/' or '\\' bond-direction tags anywhere in NATURAL_PRODUCTS_DATA. I quantified this with RDKit FindPotentialStereo on each parseable string and compared against the PubChem reference:

  Ginsenoside Rg1 — reference has 21 defined stereo elements; app.js has 0 specified and 22 unspecified => the string denotes 2^22 = 4,194,304 stereoisomers.
  Ginkgolide B   — reference has 11 defined; app.js has 0 specified, 12 unspecified => 2^12 = 4,096 stereoisomers.
  Asiatic acid   — reference has 12 defined; app.js has 0 specified, 12 unspecified => 2^12 = 4,096 stereoisomers.
  Baicalein      — achiral, so no loss here.
  Curcumin       — even after repairing the OCH3 typo, both (1E,6E) descriptors are absent => 2^2 = 4 geometric isomers.
  Huperzine A, Salvianolic acid B, Onjisaponin V — unparseable, so stereochemistry is moot (references carry 3 and 5 defined elements respectively).

This is a systematic omission across the whole dataset, not an isolated slip.

It is also a directly contradicted claim. index.html:118 advertises the natural-products tab as providing 'Detailed SMILES formulation, pharmacophoric moieties, receptor binding residue coordinates, and stereochemistry'. There is no stereochemistry anywhere in the file. Consequence: For a pentacyclic triterpenoid or a dammarane saponin, stereochemistry is not decoration — it is the molecule. Asiatic acid is specifically 2-alpha,3-beta,23-trihydroxyurs-12-en-28-oic acid; the 2-alpha,3-beta relative configuration on the A ring determines the hydrogen-bonding geometry of the diol, and a 2-beta,3-alpha diastereomer is a different compound with different target engagement. Of the 4,096 stereoisomers the app.js asiatic acid string denotes, exactly one is asiatic acid; 4,095 are not, and most are not natural products at all. For Rg1 the ratio is one in 4.2 million.

Every downstream claim in the platform is 3D: 'in-depth analysis of cation-pi anchoring, hydrophobic cage insertion' (index.html:92), binding-residue contact lists (app.js:12, 22, 32, 42, 52, 62, 72, 82), and binding free energies to one decimal place (app.js:146 etc.). None of these are defined for a flat graph. You cannot dock, cannot compute a shape or pharmacophore overlay, cannot assign a binding pose, and cannot compute a DeltaG for an undefined stereoisomer — the answer differs between diastereomers by orders of magnitude in affinity. A platform that calls itself 'structural pharmacology' while carrying no stereochemistry has no structural layer at all.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-04: Adopt isomeric SMILES from PubChem for all eight compounds and make stereochemical completeness a hard schema constraint: in the validation gate, run RDKit FindPotentialStereo on every structure and fail the build if any element returns Unspecified. Store and assert the full 27-character InChIKey (not just the 14-character skeleton block), since the second block is exactly what encodes stereochemistry — the reference asiatic acid key is JXSVIVRDWWRQRT-UYDOISQJSA-N while the flat app.js string gives JXSVIVRDWWRQRT-UHFFFAOYSA-N, and comparing only the first block would have masked this. Until stereochemistry is present, remove the claim at index.html:118 and every DeltaG and binding-pose assertion derived from these structures.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[CRITICAL] Two candidates are the amyloidogenic core of Abeta, Abeta(16-35) verbatim, presented as an anti-amyloid therapeutic with '100% fibril blockade' — The sequence at app.js:277 is 'KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLMGGGSGGSGRLVGHPW'. I matched its N-terminal segment against human Abeta1-42 (DAEFRHDSGYEVHHQKLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLMVGGVVIA) and the first 20 residues, KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM, are human Abeta(16-35) verbatim — not a fragment inspired by Abeta, but a contiguous exact copy. The same 20-mer opens AF3 candidate rank 5 at app.js:129.

That 20-mer is the aggregation engine of Abeta. It contains the KLVFF self-recognition motif (Abeta16-20), which is the nucleation element that drives beta-sheet association, together with the GAIIGLM hydrophobic stretch (Abeta29-35) that forms the second beta-strand of the cross-beta fibril core. Peptides spanning this region are the standard positive controls for spontaneous fibrillogenesis in ThT assays; they self-assemble in buffer without a template.

The platform presents this as an amyloid inhibitor. app.js:282 states it 'disrupts toxic hydrogen-bonded Abeta-AChE amyloid fibril seeding along cholinergic axonal tracts', app.js:281 asserts 'Fibril Blockade: 100%' and 'Seizure Index: 0.01', and README.md:77 labels it an 'Abeta Disruptor' delivering 'toxic Abeta-AChE seed blockade'. The declared route (app.js:279) is the basal forebrain cholinergic septal nuclei — i.e. direct CNS exposure. The genuine KLVFF-derived inhibitor literature works precisely by breaking this property: the recognition motif is kept short (KLVFF, LPFFD) and is deliberately N-methylated, D-amino-acid substituted, or capped so that it binds Abeta without extending the sheet. Appending the full GAIIGLM hydrophobic core does the opposite — it restores the self-assembly competence that inhibitor design exists to remove. Consequence: This inverts the sign of the pharmacology. The molecule described is not an anti-amyloid agent; it is a seed. Delivering Abeta(16-35) into brain parenchyma is the standard method for accelerating amyloid deposition in seeding experiments, not for clearing it. The asserted '100% fibril blockade' and 'Seizure Index: 0.01' are the exact opposite of the expected behaviour and are stated with no supporting computation anywhere in the codebase.

The integrity risk is what elevates this above an ordinary design error. The repository is presented as a drug-discovery pipeline with quantitative safety numbers, and this entry carries the same confident formatting as every other. A reader without the Abeta sequence memorised has nothing in the document that would flag it — the sequence is displayed to the user at app.js:620 as a 'FASTA Peptide / Bio-Conjugate Sequence', and index.html:362-363 offers a one-click 'Copy FASTA Sequence' button next to a 'Launch AlphaFold Server' link, actively encouraging downstream use. If any of these sequences were ever ordered from a peptide vendor on the strength of the safety table, the stated safety profile would have been actively misleading about a known neurotoxic and aggregation-competent species.

text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-05: Remove Abeta(16-35) from both records immediately. If a KLVFF-based recognition element is genuinely intended, truncate to the five-residue KLVFF motif and apply an explicit anti-aggregation modification (backbone N-methylation of alternating residues, or D-amino-acid substitution), state that modification in the chemStruct field, and delete the 'Fibril Blockade: 100%' and 'Seizure Index' assertions until an actual ThT kinetics or aggregation-propensity computation exists to support them. Add an automated screen over every sequence in the dataset that flags exact substring matches against known amyloidogenic segments (Abeta, alpha-synuclein NAC, IAPP, tau PHF6/PHF6*) and against an aggregation predictor such as TANGO/WALTZ/AGGRESCAN, and fail the build on any hit.

Established beta-sheet-breaker designs (iAbeta5/LPFFD, N-methylated KLVFF analogues, D-peptide variants) truncate to the recognition motif and chemically block the hydrogen-bonding face precisely to prevent the conjugate from nucleating fibrils itself.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[CRITICAL] The central 'natural-product warhead fused to a peptide' design premise is sterically impossible for the AChE-targeted candidates, measured against the crystal structures — README.md:45 states the method: 'We engineered 25 targeted bio-conjugate therapeutics by fusing minimal natural product pharmacophore warheads with AlphaFold3-optimized binding loop peptides.' For the acetylcholinesterase subset this is geometrically impossible, and the crystal structures say so quantitatively. I downloaded PDB 1VOT (TcAChE complexed with (-)-huperzine A, Raves et al. 1997) and PDB 4EY7 (human AChE with donepezil) from RCSB and measured directly:

  - Huperzine A sits at the base of the gorge, 4.78 A from the Trp84 side-chain centroid and 6.51 A from the catalytic Ser200. It is 12.58 A below the Trp279 peripheral anionic site.
  - It is enclosed by 26 protein residues within 6 A. It is fully buried, with no solvent-exposed face available for a linker.
  - The gorge axis, Trp84 (CAS) to Trp279 (PAS) side-chain centroids, is 16.12 A; Ser200 to Trp279 is 15.07 A.
  - The Tyr121/Phe330 bottleneck has a closest side-chain heavy-atom approach of 5.32 A. Subtracting two carbon van der Waals radii (1.70 A each) leaves a free aperture of roughly 1.9 A.
  - For calibration, donepezil — the canonical dual CAS/PAS binder — has a maximum intramolecular extent of 15.48 A in 4EY7. Spanning this gorge consumes an entire ~15 A small molecule.

A ~1.9 A aperture admits essentially nothing wider than a single extended aliphatic chain. The peptides attached to these warheads are 36-41 residues (app.js:153, 195, 247). An alpha-helix of 36 residues is ~54 A long and ~10-12 A in diameter including side chains; fully extended it is ~126 A. Neither can traverse a 16 A channel with a 1.9 A constriction, and there is no exit for the peptide because the warhead is buried under 26 residues.

The second half of the premise fails too. 'Minimal pharmacophore warhead' presupposes that huperzine A's pyridone is separable. Raves et al. specifically found 'surprisingly few strong direct interactions with protein residues to explain its high affinity' and attributed affinity to distributed hydrophobic contacts between the intact rigid tricycle and the aromatic residues lining the gorge. The binding energy is a property of the whole cage, not of an excisable pyridone. Excising the pyridone and amide-coupling it to a peptide (app.js:152, 'Huperzine A Pyridone Core (C15H18N2O) + Cys-Lys Amide Coupling') both discards the contacts that produce the affinity and consumes the ring nitrogen and the exocyclic amine that make the remaining contacts. Note also that the formula given for the 'pyridone core' fragment, C15H18N2O, is the formula of intact huperzine A — the record simultaneously claims a minimal fragment and quotes the whole molecule's formula.

app.js:154 makes the impossibility explicit by asserting the conjugate occupies 'AChE CAS (Trp84, Phe330, Tyr121) & PAS (Trp286, Tyr72, Tyr341)' simultaneously, and app.js:252 claims it 'completely blocks acetylcholine degradation' while elevating synaptic ACh by 350%. Consequence: This is the platform's stated method, applied to at least five of the twenty-five candidates and to the #1 and #7 ranked AF3 candidates (app.js:125, 131). If the paradigm is geometrically impossible for its flagship application, the ranked leaderboard and the DeltaG values attached to it are not weak estimates — they are describing binding events that cannot occur. An expert who takes README.md:45 at face value would conclude that a workable conjugation strategy had been identified for a target class where the buried-ligand problem is precisely the known, hard, unsolved obstacle. Genuine dual-site AChE inhibitors solve it the only way the geometry allows: a single small molecule long enough to span the gorge, tethered through a slim aliphatic or aromatic linker, never a polypeptide.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-06: Retract the peptide-conjugation strategy for all AChE-gorge-directed candidates (app.js:151-158, 193-200, 245-252, 285-292) and for AF3 candidates ranked 1 and 7. If dual CAS/PAS engagement is the goal, redesign as a small-molecule bivalent ligand: keep huperzine A intact as the CAS-binding unit, attach a slim linker of the length the measured 16 A span requires, and cap it with an aromatic PAS binder. Before asserting any binding mode, dock the actual proposed structure into 1VOT or 4EY7 and report the pose, the clash census, and the buried surface area — a single docking run against the real coordinates would have caught this. More generally, add a steric feasibility gate to the pipeline: for every conjugate, check whether the warhead's binding site is solvent-accessible in the target structure, and reject designs whose linker must pass through a buried channel.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Ground truth for MEDCHEM-06: Raves ML, Harel M, Pang YP, Silman I, Kozikowski AP, Sussman JL. Structure of acetylcholinesterase complexed with the nootropic alkaloid, (-)-huperzine A. Nat Struct Biol 1997;4(1):57-63 (PMID 8989325, DOI 10.1038/nsb0197-57) — establishes that huperzine A binds at the gorge base with affinity distributed over hydrophobic contacts with the aromatic gorge lining rather than a few separable strong interactions. Coordinates: PDB 1VOT (TcAChE + huperzine A) and PDB 4EY7 (human AChE + donepezil), both measured in this session. Measured geometry: CAS-PAS separation 16.1 A, Tyr121/Phe330 bottleneck free aperture ~1.9 A, huperzine A enclosed by 26 residues within 6 A, donepezil maximum extent 15.5 A. The design idiom that actually works for CAS+PAS dual occupancy is a small-molecule bivalent ligand (tacrine-donepezil hybrids, bis-tacrines) with a slim polymethylene tether sized to the ~15 A span.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[BLOCKER] Every conjugate is a 3.5-6.1 kDa polycationic peptide that cannot reach the CNS, while the uniformly asserted hERG-based safety profile assesses the wrong liability entirely — I computed the mass of every conjugate from its sequence using standard average residue masses plus water, and added the true PubChem mass of each declared warhead less water per conjugation bond. Results for the 22 of 25 records with a parseable sequence:

  Conjugate MW range 3,538 - 6,137 Da, median 4,804 Da.
  22 of 22 exceed the Ro5 500 Da limit. 22 of 22 exceed 1,000 Da. 22 of 22 exceed 3,000 Da.
  Largest: PfcGluN2A-LTP-P3 6,137 Da (45-mer + salvianolic acid B) and HippoTrk-Saponin-X1 6,123 Da (47-mer + Rg1 801 Da).
  Net formal charge at pH 7.4 reaches +9 (app.js:153 and app.js:247, KWWKFLRRFWRRLKKYFEELWKKLAEKYFELLKKYG).
  17 of 22 carry two or more free cysteines and 14 of 22 carry four or more, with no disulfide connectivity specified anywhere — an unconstrained 8-cysteine 47-mer (app.js:143) has 105 possible disulfide pairings and will scramble.
  Three records have no computable mass at all: app.js:173 and app.js:371 contain 'B', the Asx ambiguity code and not a standard residue (also at app.js:130 in AF3 candidate rank 6, which the UI offers for submission to AlphaFold Server); app.js:381 contains the literal placeholder 'His14-Phe174-Linker-Peptide-Conjugate' in the sequence field.

These numbers are 8-13x above the passive BBB permeation ceiling. The CNS MPO framework (Wager et al.) places desirable CNS agents at MW below ~360 Da with TPSA under ~90 A^2 and HBD at or below 3; peptides of this size have TPSA in the many hundreds of A^2 and dozens of backbone HBDs. Yet every record asserts a specific CNS parenchymal compartment ('CNS -> Brain -> Hippocampus (CA1/CA3 Pyramidal Neurons & DG SGZ Neural Stem Cells)', app.js:145) and quantitative pharmacodynamics (LTP +280%, app.js:148). No BBB transport mechanism — receptor-mediated transcytosis, a shuttle peptide, an efflux assessment — appears anywhere in the repository.

The safety section is worse than absent; it assesses the wrong liability. Grep shows all 25 safety fields carry the identical string 'hERG IC50 > 50 uM', and README.md:99 explains it as 'Hydrophobic peptide linkers sterically prevent binding to hERG pore Tyr652/Phe656'. A value identical across 25 chemically distinct entities is a constant, not a prediction. And hERG is not the liability here: hERG block is a small-molecule lipophilic-amine problem, and a 5 kDa polycation was never going to enter the channel inner cavity. The actual liability is the one the sequences are built from. I computed Eisenberg consensus hydrophobic moment on a 100-degree helical wheel for the recurring scaffold KWWKFLRRFWRRLKKYFEELWKKLAEKYFELLKKYG (app.js:153, app.js:247, and AF3 rank 7 at app.js:131): <muH> = 0.615 at net charge +9. Melittin, the reference bee-venom lytic peptide, scores <muH> = 0.353 at +5; magainin 2 scores 0.455 at +3. The design scores substantially higher on both axes than the canonical membrane-lytic peptides. The related 32-mer at app.js:329, labelled an 'LC3 motif', scores 0.578 at +7. Cationic amphipathic helices in this regime are hemolytic and cytolytic; that is the toxicity that needed assessing, and it is not mentioned anywhere. Instead app.js:239 asserts 'Systemic Toxicity: Negligible' and app.js:291 a 'Safety Plasticity Score: 99.5 / 100'. Consequence: This invalidates the pipeline as a therapeutics pipeline rather than merely weakening it. None of the 25 molecules can reach the compartment its own record names, so every efficacy number in the file describes an exposure that cannot occur. Simultaneously, the safety table directs a reader's attention to a liability these molecules do not have while remaining silent on the one they demonstrably do — and the numbers are asserted with two-significant-figure precision ('Seizure Index: 0.01', 'Inflammatory Cytokine Suppression: 98%', 'Downregulation: < 3.5%') that implies computation. Grep confirms no ADMET calculation of any kind exists in the codebase. A reader — particularly a non-medicinal-chemist evaluating this as a portfolio or a funding case — would conclude that 25 CNS-penetrant candidates had cleared cardiotoxicity screening. The opposite is true on both counts.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-07: Delete every asserted ADMET number in app.js:147-395 and README.md:96-102 — they are constants, not predictions — and replace them with values actually computed and labelled with the method and version that produced them. Compute, per candidate: MW, TPSA, HBD/HBA and cLogP/cLogD from the real structure via RDKit; a CNS MPO desirability score; net charge and Eisenberg hydrophobic moment with an explicit hemolysis/cytolysis flag for any sequence exceeding the melittin reference; predicted immunogenicity (MHC-II binding); and plasma/protease stability. Fix the three malformed sequences (remove 'B' at app.js:130/173/371, replace the placeholder at app.js:381) and specify disulfide connectivity for every multi-cysteine design. Then either state an explicit BBB delivery mechanism with supporting evidence, or restate the target compartment honestly as peripheral. Replace the hERG claim with a liability assessment appropriate to polycationic amphipathic peptides.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Ground truth for MEDCHEM-07: Wager TT, Hou X, Verhoest PR, Villalobos A. Moving beyond rules: the development of a central nervous system multiparameter optimization (CNS MPO) approach to enable alignment of druglike properties. ACS Chem Neurosci 2010;1(6):435-449 (PMID 22778837, DOI 10.1021/cn100008c), and the follow-up validation, ACS Chem Neurosci 2016;7(6):767-775 (PMID 26991242, DOI 10.1021/acschemneuro.6b00029): CNS desirability is driven by MW, TPSA, HBD, ClogP, ClogD and basic pKa; 74% of marketed CNS drugs score >=4 of 6, and the marketed CNS set sits far below 1 kDa. Peptides of 3-6 kDa with net charge up to +9 have essentially zero passive BBB permeability and require an active transcytosis mechanism. On the toxicity side, net cationic charge >= +4 combined with Eisenberg <muH> above ~0.35 is the canonical membrane-lytic pharmacophore shared by melittin (<muH> 0.353, +5) and magainin 2 (<muH> 0.455, +3), both measured here for calibration.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[MAJOR] No assay-interference assessment anywhere, though four of eight compounds are canonical interference scaffolds and curcumin is the textbook PAINS/IMPS case — Four of the eight compounds are recognised assay-interference liabilities, and the repository contains no interference discussion, no PAINS filter, no aggregation check and no counter-screen recommendation. Grep over README.md, app.js, index.html and styles.css returns zero hits for PAINS, aggregation, interference, redox, Michael acceptor or thiol reactivity.

Curcumin is the strongest case in the modern medicinal chemistry literature. Nelson et al. (J Med Chem 2017) classify it as both a PAINS and an IMPS (invalid metabolic panacea) candidate and conclude it is 'an unstable, reactive, nonbioavailable compound and, therefore, a highly improbable lead', noting that more than 120 clinical trials have run and that no double-blinded placebo-controlled trial of curcumin has succeeded. The mechanistic basis is exactly what the platform relies on: the bis-alpha,beta-unsaturated 1,3-diketone is a promiscuous Michael acceptor, it undergoes rapid hydrolytic degradation above pH 7, it redox-cycles, it is fluorescent and interferes with fluorescence-based readouts, it chelates metals, and it aggregates. The platform reports these liabilities as the mechanism of action: app.js:54 and README.md:36 present 'Keap1 Cys151 Alkylation' as the therapeutic mechanism. Covalent alkylation of a reactive cysteine by a promiscuous Michael acceptor is exactly the reactivity that makes curcumin non-selective — Cys151 is one of many thiols it will hit. Presenting non-selective thiol reactivity as targeted pharmacology, with no cysteine-selectivity data and no thiol-reactivity counter-screen, is the specific reasoning error the PAINS literature exists to correct. Curcumin is nevertheless deployed as a warhead in three candidates (app.js:162, 298, 338).

Baicalein (or rather the 6,7,8-triol actually encoded, per MEDCHEM-02) is a polyphenol with an ortho-triol: catechol and pyrogallol motifs auto-oxidise at physiological pH to generate quinones and hydrogen peroxide, which inactivate enzymes non-specifically — a particularly acute concern for the claimed 12/15-LOX iron target and for the cysteine-containing GSK-3beta. Salvianolic acid B carries four catechol rings by the platform's own description (app.js:75) and has cLogP and polyphenol character consistent with colloidal aggregation. Asiatic acid computes to cLogP 5.03 with MW 489 by RDKit here — squarely in the physicochemical regime the Aggregation Advisor flags as aggregation-prone.

None of this appears. The compounds are presented with clean, specific residue-level binding claims (app.js:42, 52, 72, 82) as though selectivity were established. Consequence: The entire Section 1 pharmacophore matrix rests on literature target assignments for compounds whose reported activities are, for a substantial fraction, artefacts of the assay format rather than genuine target engagement. Building 25 conjugate designs on those warheads propagates the artefact into the design layer: if curcumin's Keap1 engagement is non-selective thiol alkylation, a curcumin-peptide conjugate inherits the non-selectivity and gains nothing. A medicinal chemist reading README.md:36 would see a well-known IMPS presented as a validated Nrf2 mechanism with no caveat, and would immediately discount the credibility of the whole matrix — which is unfortunate, because parts of the pharmacology narrative are qualitatively sound (see the overall assessment). Honest treatment of the interference liability would cost the document nothing and would substantially raise its credibility with the audience it is aimed at.

text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-08: Run RDKit's PAINS_A/B/C filter catalogue over all eight structures once they parse, and surface every alert in the UI alongside the compound rather than in a footnote. Add an explicit interference-liability field to each natural-product record covering Michael-acceptor reactivity, redox cycling, metal chelation, assay fluorescence, aggregation propensity (cross-checked against the Aggregation Advisor) and chemical stability at pH 7.4. For curcumin specifically, cite Nelson et al. 2017 in the record and either drop it as a warhead or state explicitly what selectivity evidence supports the Keap1 Cys151 claim over the many other reactive thiols in the proteome. Where a target claim rests on a reported activity, require the standard counter-screens (detergent control for aggregation, thiol-reactivity counter-screen, orthogonal non-fluorescent readout) to be cited or flag the claim as unvalidated.

text:
[MAJOR] AChE binding-site residue lists are chimeras of Torpedo and human numbering; no single ortholog has the residue set claimed — The AChE residue numbers throughout the platform mix two organisms' conventions, sometimes inside a single string. I verified the actual residue identities by parsing CA records from the two crystal structures.

PDB 1VOT (Torpedo californica AChE): residue 70 = TYR, 72 = ASP, 84 = TRP, 121 = TYR, 279 = TRP, 330 = PHE, 334 = TYR, 200 = SER, 440 = HIS.
PDB 4EY7 (human AChE): residue 72 = TYR, 74 = ASP, 86 = TRP, 121 = GLY, 124 = TYR, 286 = TRP, 330 = VAL, 337 = TYR, 338 = PHE, 341 = TYR, 203 = SER, 447 = HIS.

So Trp84/Phe330/Tyr121/Trp279 are Torpedo numbering, and Trp286/Tyr72/Tyr341 are human numbering. app.js:154 states 'AChE CAS (Trp84, Phe330, Tyr121) & PAS (Trp286, Tyr72, Tyr341)' — Torpedo CAS concatenated with human PAS in one field. app.js:248 does the same: 'AChE Catalytic Gorge (Trp84, Phe330, Trp286, Tyr341)'. app.js:288 pairs them explicitly as 'CAS/PAS (Trp84/Trp286)'. README.md:32 mixes them in a single sentence: 'CAS: Trp84, Phe330 & PAS (Trp286)'.

There is no acetylcholinesterase for which any of these lists is correct. In human AChE, residue 121 is glycine and residue 330 is valine, so 'Phe330, Tyr121' is simply wrong. In Torpedo AChE, residue 286 is not tryptophan and 341 is not tyrosine, so 'Trp286, Tyr341' is wrong. Separately, app.js:12 describes the Trp84 interaction as a 'CAS Salt Bridge'; Trp84 is a tryptophan with no ionisable side chain and cannot form a salt bridge. The same file correctly identifies the interaction as cation-pi at app.js:15 and README.md:32, so the file contradicts itself on the interaction type as well as the numbering. Consequence: Residue numbers are the interface between this document and any structural work someone does downstream. Anyone loading a human AChE structure and looking for Phe330 finds a valine; anyone loading Torpedo and looking for Trp286 finds the wrong residue. Because the two systems are offset by only 2-8 residues in this region, the errors are quiet — a modeller may select a nearby residue and believe the mapping worked. The correspondences are well established and unambiguous, so this is straightforwardly fixable, but as written the binding-site definitions cannot be used and the 'CAS Salt Bridge' error signals that the interaction types were not checked either.

text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-09: Pick one numbering convention — human AChE (UniProt P22303, mature-protein numbering as in PDB 4EY7) is the right choice for a therapeutics platform — and convert every residue reference in app.js:12, 15, 72, 154, 248, 278, 288 and README.md:32, 38 to it. Add an explicit 'numbering: UniProt P22303 / PDB 4EY7' annotation to each binding-site field so the convention is never ambiguous again, and validate residue identities programmatically against the reference structure at build time. Correct 'CAS Salt Bridge' at app.js:12 to 'cation-pi'.

text: Ground truth for MEDCHEM-09: Verified from coordinate files this session. Torpedo californica AChE (PDB 1VOT): CAS Trp84, Tyr130, Phe330, Phe331; catalytic triad Ser200/His440/Glu327; PAS Tyr70, Asp72, Tyr121, Trp279, Tyr334. Human AChE (PDB 4EY7): CAS Trp86, Tyr133, Tyr337, Phe338; catalytic triad Ser203/His447/Glu334; PAS Tyr72, Asp74, Tyr124, Trp286, Tyr341. Equivalences: Torpedo Trp84 = human Trp86; Phe330 = Tyr337; Trp279 = Trp286; Tyr70 = Tyr72; Tyr121 = Tyr124; Asp72 = Asp74. Trp84/Trp86 engages quaternary ammonium and protonated amines by cation-pi interaction, not a salt bridge (Raves et al. 1997, PMID 8989325).

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text:
[MAJOR] No chemistry layer exists: no structure validation, canonicalization, InChIKey, database cross-reference, or computed property anywhere in the codebase — The repository presents itself as a cheminformatics platform but contains no cheminformatics. Chemical structures exist only as display strings: app.js:477 interpolates `${data.smiles}` into innerHTML inside a div labelled 'SMILES Formulation'. There is no parser, no canonicalizer, no identifier, no cross-reference and no computed descriptor. Every chemical property presented to the user — molecular formulas in the chemStruct fields, DeltaG values, Kd values, ADMET numbers — is a hand-typed literal in the data structure, not a computed quantity. This is the root cause that permitted MEDCHEM-01 through MEDCHEM-04 and MEDCHEM-08: with no validation pass, a token typo, a missing ring closure, two formula strings, a wrong isomer, two wrong constitutions and universally absent stereochemistry all reached a published repository undetected.

The absence is verifiable rather than inferred: the grep above returns hits only in unrelated directories (memory/SPEC_draft.md, research/memory_systems/surveys.json) and never in the four platform files.

This is worth stating separately from the individual errors because fixing the errors one at a time leaves the mechanism that produced them intact. Consequence: Without a validation layer, every future edit can reintroduce the same class of defect silently, and there is no way for a reader to distinguish a computed value from a typed one — which is the core epistemic problem with the document. Adding the layer is cheap: I installed RDKit into a fresh venv and validated all eight structures against PubChem in a few minutes of wall-clock time in this session, which is the same work the project would need to do once and then run in CI. The gap between what the platform claims ('AI-driven drug discovery platform', README.md:22) and what it implements (a static data-display page) is bridged almost entirely by this one missing component.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Required fix for MEDCHEM-10: Introduce a chemistry module with a build-time gate that, for every compound record, (1) parses the SMILES with RDKit and fails on None; (2) runs the ChEMBL structure_pipeline Checker and Standardizer; (3) computes the full 27-character InChIKey and asserts it against a stored PubChem/ChEMBL reference, failing on mismatch — this single check catches MEDCHEM-02 and MEDCHEM-03; (4) asserts zero Unspecified elements from FindPotentialStereo — this catches MEDCHEM-04; (5) runs the PAINS_A/B/C FilterCatalog and surfaces alerts — this catches MEDCHEM-08; (6) computes MW, formula, TPSA, cLogP, HBD/HBA, rotatable bonds and CNS MPO, and renders those computed values in the UI in place of the hand-typed strings. Store PubChem CID and ChEMBL ID as required fields on every record. Mark every remaining asserted value in the UI with a provenance tag distinguishing computed from literature-cited from estimated, so the reader can tell them apart.

text: Ground truth for MEDCHEM-10: Bento AP, Hersey A, Felix E, Landrum G, Gaulton A, Atkinson F, Bellis LJ, De Veij M, Leach AR. An open source chemical structure curation pipeline using RDKit. J Cheminform 2020;12(1):51 (PMID 33431044, DOI 10.1186/s13321-020-00456-1) — the reference implementation, comprising a Checker that tests structure validity and flags serious errors, a Standardizer that normalises to defined conventions, and a GetParent component; used to standardise the ~2 million compounds in ChEMBL and freely available on GitHub and via ChEMBL Beaker. RDKit (https://github.com/rdkit/rdkit) provides MolFromSmiles, MolToSmiles canonicalization, MolToInchiKey, CalcMolFormula, FindPotentialStereo, the Descriptors module and the PAINS FilterCatalog. PubChem PUG-REST and the ChEMBL API provide identity verification by name, InChIKey or connectivity SMILES.

text:
[MINOR] Onjisaponin V is conflated with DISS, a structurally unrelated compound, and its formula does not match the reference record — app.js:58 names a single record 'Onjisaponin V / DISS' and app.js:59 gives its class as 'Triterpenoid Saponin & Oligosaccharide Ester', treating the two names as synonyms for one substance. They are different compounds from different structural classes. DISS is 3,6'-disinapoyl sucrose (PubChem CID 131752949), C34H42O19, MW 754.7 — a disaccharide bis-cinnamate ester with no triterpene at all. Onjisaponin V is a presenegenin-based triterpenoid saponin. Both occur in Polygala tenuifolia, which is presumably the source of the confusion, but they share neither a skeleton nor a mechanism. The record then assigns one merged set of targets and mechanisms (app.js:61-65) to the pair.

Separately, the formula placed in the SMILES field at app.js:60, C58H92O27, does not match the PubChem record for onjisaponin V (CID 177827987, C82H122O41, MW 1763.8). I note that onjisaponin nomenclature is inconsistent across sources, so I hold this specific formula discrepancy at lower confidence than the DISS conflation.

The derived aglycone formula is also wrong and is stated twice: app.js:182 and app.js:328 give 'Presenegenin Aglycone (C30H46O6)' where PubChem CID 21594224 gives presenegenin as C30H46O7, MW 518.7 — one oxygen short. Consequence: The conflated record drives two candidate designs (HippoDual-TrkB-AMPK-X5 at app.js:181-188 and MicroAutophagy-Tag-M4 at app.js:327-334), both of which declare a presenegenin aglycone warhead with an incorrect formula. A reader trying to source or synthesise the warhead would order against the wrong formula, and a reader trying to trace the AMPK/autophagy mechanism claimed at app.js:64 would find it attributed in the literature to one of these two compounds and not the other. This is the least consequential of the findings and is straightforward to correct, but it compounds the general pattern that no chemical identifier in this repository was checked against a reference database.

text: The Essential Medicinal Chemistry of Curcumin (2017). The definitive assessment of curcumin as simultaneously a PAINS and an IMPS (invalid metabolic panacea) candidate. Documents that curcumin is unstable above pH 7, reactive as a promiscuous Michael acceptor, redox-active, fluorescent, metal-chelating, aggregation-prone and essentially non-bioavailable orally, and records that despite >120 clinical trials no double-blinded placebo-controlled trial has succeeded. Concludes it is 'a highly improbable lead'. Application here: Directly governs the curcumin record at app.js:48-55 and README.md:36, and the three candidates that use curcumin as a warhead (app.js:162, 298, 338). The platform presents 'Keap1 Cys151 Alkylation' as targeted pharmacology; this paper establishes that the alkylation is non-selective Michael reactivity and is the mechanism of curcumin's assay promiscuity, not of a selective therapeutic effect. Cite it in the record and either drop curcumin as a warhead or supply cysteine-selectivity data and a thiol-reactivity counter-screen.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: New substructure filters for removal of pan assay interference compounds (PAINS) from screening libraries and for their exclusion in bioassays (2010). The original PAINS substructure alert set that identifies frequent-hitter scaffolds not caught by conventional reactive-compound filters, and the argument that such compounds are increasingly prevalent in the literature as apparent leads when they are not. Implemented directly in RDKit as FilterCatalogParams.FilterCatalogs.PAINS_A/B/C. Application here: Older than the 10-year window but load-bearing as the ground truth for MEDCHEM-08. Provides the runnable filter to add to the validation gate specified in MEDCHEM-10: once the eight structures parse, running the RDKit PAINS catalogue over them gives an automated, reproducible interference flag per compound to surface in the UI. The curcuminoid and catechol/pyrogallol polyphenol scaffolds in this dataset are exactly what the alert set targets.

source.ref: PMID:8989325 / DOI:10.1038/nsb0197-57 (Nat Struct Biol 4(1):57-63); coordinates PDB 1VOT

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Structure of acetylcholinesterase complexed with the nootropic alkaloid, (-)-huperzine A (1997). The 2.5 A crystal structure of the huperzine A-AChE complex, showing an unexpected binding orientation with 'surprisingly few strong direct interactions with protein residues to explain its high affinity', and demonstrating through SAR on structural analogues that the affinity arises from distributed hydrophobic contacts between the intact rigid tricycle and the aromatic residues lining the active-site gorge. Application here: The ground truth for MEDCHEM-06 and MEDCHEM-09. It refutes the 'minimal pharmacophore warhead' premise at README.md:45 and app.js:152 — huperzine A's affinity is not localised in an excisable pyridone. The deposited coordinates are what I measured to obtain the gorge geometry (CAS-PAS 16.1 A, Tyr121/Phe330 free aperture ~1.9 A, ligand enclosed by 26 residues) and the authoritative Torpedo residue numbering. Any redesign should dock the actual proposed conjugate into 1VOT or 4EY7 and report the pose and clash census before asserting a binding mode.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: An open source chemical structure curation pipeline using RDKit (2020). The ChEMBL structure curation pipeline: a Checker that tests chemical validity and flags serious structural errors, a Standardizer that normalises structures to defined conventions, and a GetParent component that strips salts and solvents. Used to standardise the ~2 million compounds in ChEMBL; freely available on GitHub and through ChEMBL Beaker webservices. Application here: The reference implementation for the missing chemistry layer in MEDCHEM-10, and the single change that would have prevented MEDCHEM-01 through MEDCHEM-04. Running the Checker over NATURAL_PRODUCTS_DATA would immediately flag the four unparseable strings; adding an InChIKey assertion against PubChem would have caught the baicalein isomer swap and the Rg1/Ginkgolide B constitution errors, which molecular-formula checking alone cannot detect.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: An Aggregation Advisor for Ligand Discovery (2015). Establishes colloidal aggregation as the dominant mechanism of artifactual protein inhibition and provides a predictive tool (advisor.bkslab.org) that scores aggregation likelihood from lipophilicity, affinity and similarity to a database of >12,000 known aggregators. Reports that 5.1% of ligands active in the 0.1-10 uM range in the medicinal chemistry literature resemble known aggregators, versus only 0.73% of drug-like commercial compounds — i.e. aggregators are strongly enriched in the published literature. Application here: Supports MEDCHEM-08 for the polyphenol and lipophilic-triterpenoid members of the set. Asiatic acid computes here to cLogP 5.03 at MW 489, and salvianolic acid B is a four-catechol polyphenol — both in the physicochemical regime the advisor flags. Run each validated structure through the advisor and record the score in the interference-liability field; require a detergent-control counter-screen before accepting any reported potency for these compounds.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Moving beyond rules: the development of a central nervous system multiparameter optimization (CNS MPO) approach to enable alignment of druglike properties (2010). The CNS MPO desirability algorithm built on six physicochemical parameters (ClogP, ClogD7.4, MW, TPSA, HBD, most basic pKa), validated against 119 marketed CNS drugs, 108 Pfizer CNS candidates and 11,303 diversity compounds. 74% of marketed CNS drugs score >=4 of 6, and higher scores track with favourable permeability, lower P-gp efflux, metabolic stability and safety. Application here: The quantitative standard against which the 3,538-6,137 Da polycationic conjugates of MEDCHEM-07 fail by roughly an order of magnitude on MW alone, before TPSA and HBD are considered. Implement CNS MPO scoring in the validation gate and display the score per candidate; this replaces the asserted-constant ADMET table at app.js:147-395 with a computed, reproducible, method-labelled number.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Central Nervous System Multiparameter Optimization Desirability: Application in Drug Discovery (2016). Prospective validation of CNS MPO on a second wave of candidates designed after the tool's implementation, showing improved ADME alignment, better BBB penetration, residence in lower-risk safety space (low ClogP, high TPSA), fewer compounds sent to exploratory toxicology, and improved survival through regulatory toxicology into first-in-human. Application here: Demonstrates that prospective multiparameter scoring, rather than post hoc assertion, is what moves CNS candidates forward — the exact discipline missing from Section 3 of the README. Use it to justify replacing the uniform 'hERG IC50 > 50 uM' constant with a computed desirability profile plus liability flags appropriate to the actual modality.

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: Curcumin May (Not) Defy Science (2017). The authors' response to community pushback on the 2017 J Med Chem review, reinforcing and clarifying the evidentiary basis for classifying curcumin as an improbable lead. Application here: Useful as the companion citation when documenting the curcumin liability in the compound record, since it addresses the counterarguments a reader is most likely to raise.

source.ref: https://github.com/rdkit/rdkit (version 2026.3.5, installed and used in this session)

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: RDKit: Open-source cheminformatics toolkit (2026). SMILES parsing and canonicalization, InChI/InChIKey generation, molecular formula and exact/average mass, FindPotentialStereo for stereochemical completeness auditing, the Descriptors module (MolLogP, TPSA, HBD/HBA, rotatable bonds), SMARTS substructure matching, and the PAINS FilterCatalog. Application here: This is the tool I used to produce every structural claim in this review, and it is the concrete implementation vehicle for the validation gate in MEDCHEM-10. The entire audit — parsing all eight strings, computing formulas and InChIKeys, counting unspecified stereo elements, and diffing against PubChem references — took a few minutes in a fresh venv, which is the full cost of the missing chemistry layer.

source.ref: PDB:4EY7 (RCSB; coordinate file downloaded and parsed in this session)

tags: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
text: PDB 4EY7: Crystal structure of recombinant human acetylcholinesterase in complex with donepezil (2012). Human AChE coordinates giving the authoritative human residue numbering (Trp86, Tyr72, Tyr124, Trp286, Tyr337, Phe338, Tyr341, Ser203, His447) and a bound dual-site inhibitor whose maximum intramolecular extent I measured at 15.48 A. Application here: Ground truth for MEDCHEM-09 (it is what shows that human residue 121 is Gly and 330 is Val, falsifying the mixed residue lists at app.js:154 and app.js:248) and the calibration point for MEDCHEM-06: donepezil demonstrates that spanning the CAS-PAS gorge consumes an entire ~15 A small molecule, which is the design idiom a bivalent AChE inhibitor must use instead of a 36-mer peptide.
